newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE - South Korea's chaebols head for Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - South Korea's chaebols head for Vietnam.

text.p: After several years of at times stormy relations between South Korean firms and their employees in Vietnam, a charm offensive appears to be under way to help improve growing trade ties between the two nations.

"Unlike other investors, Daewoo came to us as a friend and brother, helping us improve our career and our lives," an employee of the luxury Hanoi Daewoo Hotel enthuses in the blurb of an eye-catching magazine advertisement.
But relations between between other South Korean firms and their employees have not always been so cosy.

In August, a Vietnamese court sentenced a South Korean factory supervisor to a three-month suspended prison term on charges of labour abuse. She was reported to have hit 15 workers on the head with a shoe.
A few months earlier, a South Korean man was expelled from Vietnam for beating up a taxi driver and then making him kneel and beg for mercy after a quarrel over his fare.
And yet, when South Korean President Kim Young-sam makes his first official visit to Vietnam this week, friendship, brotherhood -- and big business -- are likely to be high on the agenda.

"President Kim will give an important speech ... calling for expansion of cooperation in the field of industry and business between the two countries," Seoul's ambassador to Vietnam, Kim Bong-kyu, told the Lao Dong newspaper.
Both sides say there are no hard feelings from the Vietnam War, when Seoul's forces fought against North Vietnam alongside the U.S.-backed Saigon administration.
Seoul's ties with Vietnam were cut when communist forces won the war in 1975, and it established diplomatic relations with Hanoi only in 1992.
South Korea is now Vietnam's third-biggest trading partner; trade between the two countries was $1.54 billion last year, a three-fold increase from 1992.

Korean companies have earmarked some $2.3 billion for 169 projects in Vietnam and, with some big ventures in the oil and manufacturing sectors in the pipeline, that figure looks set to jump over the next few months.

The Daewoo Group is the biggest single foreign investor in Vietnam, with approval for ventures worth $725 million, and according to a government-run magazine report it is ready to more than double that commitment.

Daewoo is one of several South Korean industrial conglomerates, known at home as "chaebols", which are making a push to get a foothold in the nascent markets of an economy in rapid transition. These include Samsung Group, LG Group and Hyundai Group

"Vietnam is an attractive place to invest in because of cheap labour and good potential for growth," said Kim Hee-chin, director of the economic cooperation division at the South Korean Ministry of Finance and Economy.

Park Can-shin, director of the Ho Chi Minh City-based Korea Trade Centre, a governmental trade and investment promotion agency, says the advantages of low labour costs and political stability easily outweigh the disadvantages.
South Korean firms' enthusiasm comes at a time when others are expressing frustration over the problems of doing business in a country whose drive for reform promised so much.
Huge bureaucracy, rampant corruption and an inadequate legal and regulatory framework have all, according to a senior banker in Hanoi, "taken the bloom off the rose".

Pham Chi Lan, Secretary General of the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said chaebols like Daewoo tended to have a more long-term perspective on Vietnam than other foreign firms, not expecting to turn profits overnight.
Despite the growing special business relationship, though, a cultural divide between the two countries still sometimes rears its head in ugly labour disputes.
"The customs of the two nations are vastly different," ambassador Kim conceded in a magazine interview last year.

"In Korea, the fact that a superintendent becomes irritated and shouts at the workers is considered a normal thing," he said. "In Vietnam, the workers would take it as an insult and would react strongly in return."
